scope: Manual comparison of nineteen foundational interfaces from the change-point regression paper against the pinned mathlib declarations; preserve the frozen source statements and distinct stationary, nonstationary, marginal and directional assumptions.

rows.query: rg -i 'functional dependence|sub.?weibull|stationar.*causal|bernoulli shift' Mathlib/Probability Mathlib/Dynamics; inspect iIndepFun in Independence/Basic, IdentDistrib and Measurable with their ambient measure parameters
rows.result: The checked declarations express jointly independent innovations, their identical laws and a measurable vector-valued generator; no verified packaged causal Bernoulli-shift construction or stationarity theorem was located.
rows.gap: Construct the lag-indexed innovation histories and prove strict stationarity of their common measurable image.

comparisons.D5: Use integer-indexed random elements for script X, joint independence under one probability law and IdentDistrib for their common marginal law; G is one time-invariant measurable map into p-dimensional real vectors. Histories must be identified by relative lag before applying the same G. Plain X denotes the resulting observed process, not the innovation. Measurability and iid primitives alone do not supply the history construction or the equality of all finite-dimensional shifted laws asserted as strict stationarity.

rows.query: Inspect Probability/Moments/Covariance covariance definition and Probability/IdentDistrib structure; compare finite-coordinate population moments with the source's causal infinite sequence
rows.result: Scalar covariance can define each entry of the population matrix and identical distributions express equality of marginal laws; neither declaration packages a mean-zero stationary causal triangular sequence.
rows.gap: Assemble the mean-zero causal covariate sequence, its consecutive observation window and its integrable coordinate covariance matrix for each sample size.

comparisons.D12: Set Sigma i j to covariance of coordinates i and j of X_1, under the population probability measure, and supply the moments required for an ordinary covariance interpretation. The n observations are consecutive terms of an integer-indexed process of form (4), with zero marginal mean. IdentDistrib describes marginal equality but does not establish joint strict stationarity. The dimension p and population law may vary with n; Sigma is not a fixed empirical Gram matrix.

rows.query: Search Probability and Dynamics for sub-Weibull interfaces; inspect dotProduct, EuclideanSpace.norm_eq, Real.rpow, Real.exp and the boundedness/nonemptiness hypotheses of csSup_le_iff
rows.result: The directional projection, Euclidean unit sphere and exponential-power bound are expressible; the checked supremum lemma converts a bounded nonempty set of tail probabilities to all-direction inequalities, without proving such tails.
rows.gap: Define and prove the uniform sub-Weibull tail property over every Euclidean unit direction with the paper's common constants.

comparisons.D14: For every positive tau take the probability of the strict event abs(dotProduct v X_1) > tau, uniformly over norm v = 1. Gamma_2 lies in (0,2] and C_X is an absolute positive constant; real powers have positive base tau/C_X here. Real-valued probabilities are bounded by one under a probability measure, but nonemptiness of the unit sphere also needs positive dimension before using csSup_le_iff. Coordinatewise tails do not imply this exact uniform constant, and gamma_2 below two is not replaced by a sub-Gaussian hypothesis.

rows.query: Inspect Data/Matrix/Mul dotProduct and compare its finite coordinate sum with the complete regression and integer change-point specification
rows.result: dotProduct gives each linear predictor; the checked library declaration contains no piecewise coefficient model, endpoint convention or characterization of change locations.
rows.gap: Define the sample-size-dependent regression sequence and its ordered integer segmentation with changes exactly at the stated boundaries.

comparisons.D1: Represent y_t = dotProduct X_t beta_t + epsilon_t for t = 1,...,n with p = p(n), and deterministic coefficients constant on the integer segments [eta_k,eta_{k+1}). Preserve eta_0 = 1 and eta_{K+1} = n+1, so eta_k starts the new segment. The comparison beta_t versus beta_{t-1} is meaningful at interior indices; the displayed source only declares beta_1,...,beta_n and supplies no beta_0 for a literal t=1 reading. Do not silently add one, nor add sparsity or conditional mean-zero assumptions supplied elsewhere.

rows.query: Inspect Analysis/InnerProductSpace/PiL2 EuclideanSpace.norm_eq and compare the jump's signed indices and nonzero normalization
rows.result: The finite-dimensional Euclidean norm is directly available; the jump vector, fixed number of change points and n-dependent normalization are specific to the source model.
rows.gap: Define each signed adjacent-time coefficient jump and justify division by its positive Euclidean magnitude under the change-point model.

comparisons.D34: Psi_k is beta at eta_k minus beta at eta_k minus one time step, not beta at eta_{k-1}; the sign must be retained. Use the Euclidean norm, and scalar multiplication by its reciprocal, to obtain v_k. Actual changes imply a nonzero jump, so kappa_k is positive for every finite sample under this model. K is a fixed absolute integer at least one, while v_k and kappa_k can depend on n; no fixed direction across n is asserted.

rows.query: Inspect EuclideanSpace.norm_eq and the generated order-dual Finset.exists_min_image with its nonempty finite-domain hypothesis
rows.result: Euclidean magnitudes and attainment of a minimum on a nonempty finite index set are checked ingredients; jump and spacing bounds are model-specific assumptions.
rows.gap: Assemble the two minima over their different index sets and retain the absolute upper jump bound without inventing a uniform positive lower jump bound.

comparisons.D4: The magnitude minimum ranges over k = 1,...,K and uses norm Psi_k; the spacing minimum ranges over k = 1,...,K+1 and includes the first and last segments. K >= 1 makes both finite sets nonempty. The strict boundary ordering gives positive integer spacings, not normalized fractions. Each kappa_k is bounded above by C_kappa; positivity of finite-sample jumps does not assert a positive lower bound independent of n, and the vanishing regime remains possible.

rows.query: Inspect LinearAlgebra/Matrix/PosDef PosSemidef, Data/Matrix/Mul dotProduct and Order/Filter/Defs Tendsto; compare the covariance lower bound and directional limiting drift
rows.result: Positive-semidefinite order can express the quadratic-form lower bound for Sigma minus c_min times the identity, and Tendsto can express each scalar drift limit; the checked declarations do not prove the eigenvalue equivalence or the limits.
rows.gap: Connect the covariance eigenvalue bound to the uniform quadratic-form inequality and establish each positive directional limit along the sample-size sequence.

comparisons.D15: For a real symmetric covariance matrix, PosSemidef(Sigma - c_min I) is the appropriate form encoding, once its equivalence to the least eigenvalue condition is justified. The absolute c_min is strictly positive and applies in every direction, rather than only sparse directions. The scalar dotProduct v_k (Sigma.mulVec v_k) tends to the positive absolute varpi_k as n tends to infinity; Sigma and v_k can both vary with n. This is neither a sample covariance assertion nor a finite-n equality to varpi_k.

rows.query: Inspect MeasureTheory/Function/ConditionalExpectation/Basic condExp including its sub-sigma-algebra, sigma-finiteness and integrability branches
rows.result: The library conditional expectation supports conditioning on the sigma-algebra generated by X_t; its zero fallback must not be used as evidence for the statistical assumption.
rows.gap: Instantiate the contemporaneous covariate sigma-algebra and prove the integrable conditional expectation is almost surely zero for each observed time.

comparisons.D2: Under the regression model, condition epsilon_t on sigma(X_t) and require the resulting conditional expectation to equal zero almost surely for every t = 1,...,n. Establish the sub-sigma-algebra and integrability requirements so the library definition has its usual meaning. The source does not condition on the full past, assert independence between epsilon_t and X_t, or require independent covariate and noise innovation streams.

rows.query: Inspect Data/Finset/Filter filter and Data/Finset/Card card for finite nonzero coordinate supports
rows.result: Finite filtering and cardinality express the nonzero coordinate count; the time-indexed sparsity assumption and its supplied support sets require a source-specific predicate.
rows.gap: Define the per-time support bound and relate a chosen containing support to the cardinality of the actual nonzero coordinates.

comparisons.D3: For each time choose a finite S_t contained in the p coordinate indices, with card S_t <= s and beta_t,j = 0 outside S_t. Filtering all coordinates by beta_t,j != 0 gives the actual support and needs classical decidability for real equality if used directly. S_t can contain zero coefficients and can vary with time; the source neither fixes one common support nor bounds nonzero coefficient magnitudes away from zero.

rows.query: Inspect Order/Filter/Defs Tendsto and compare the source's per-jump vanishing regime with its finite-sample nonzero normalization
rows.result: Tendsto directly expresses a deterministic jump magnitude sequence tending to zero; it does not establish the model-specific limit or extend conclusions to another regime.
rows.gap: Supply each sample-size-indexed jump magnitude and retain the vanishing-regime restriction in the variance and inference results that use it.

comparisons.D33: For each k in the fixed finite change-point set, assert Tendsto (fun n => kappa_k(n)) atTop (nhds 0). This does not set any finite-n jump to zero or invalidate v_k normalization where changes are nonzero. The frozen source review records that Sections 4 and 4.1 restrict to this regime even though Theorems 8 and 10 refer back to the two-regime Theorem 3; the library comparison does not broaden their scope.

rows.query: Search Probability and Dynamics for stationary causal/Bernoulli-shift interfaces; inspect iIndepFun, IdentDistrib and Measurable for the noise innovation family
rows.result: Joint independence, common marginal law and a measurable scalar generator are available, but no verified declaration packages the lag history and its strict stationarity consequence.
rows.gap: Construct the scalar noise process from its own lag-indexed iid history and prove strict stationarity without adding cross-stream independence.

comparisons.D8: Observed epsilon_t is g of the history of innovation varepsilon_s for s <= t, where g is time-invariant and scalar-valued. Use a common relative-lag domain for these histories and an integer-indexed jointly independent identically distributed innovation family. The different epsilon and varepsilon symbols must stay distinct. Independence among this family's innovations does not assert independence from script-X innovations or, by itself, joint stationarity of the pair (X_t, epsilon_t).

rows.query: Search Probability and Dynamics for functional dependence; inspect Real.exp, Real.rpow and csSup_le_iff for the all-lag weighted fourth-moment bound
rows.result: The weighted bound and supremum conversion are expressible with checked real analysis primitives; no verified scalar functional-dependence decay API was found.
rows.gap: Define the noise cumulative L4 dependence coefficients and establish the uniform exponential-power bound over all nonnegative lags.

comparisons.D17: Use Delta^epsilon_{m,4} from (9), multiplied by exp(c m^gamma_1), with absolute positive c, gamma_1 and D_epsilon. The supremum is over all nonnegative integer lags, including zero, not an eventual asymptotic bound. csSup_le_iff requires a nonempty bounded-above set, so do not infer boundedness from a totalized real supremum without that condition. The common gamma notation is a worst-case convention across covariates and errors, not an assertion that their dependence coefficients coincide.

rows.query: Inspect Probability/Moments/Variance variance and its extended-moment toReal definition; inspect IdentDistrib for the scalar stationary marginals
rows.result: The real variance and equality of marginal laws are available; finite centered second moment must be supplied, and the causal stationarity and positive absolute variance are assumptions.
rows.gap: Assemble the mean-zero stationary noise subsequence with a finite positive marginal variance independent of sample size.

comparisons.D16: The observations are consecutive terms from the integer-indexed scalar process in (8), whose marginal mean is zero and variance at time 1 is the positive absolute constant sigma_epsilon squared. Library variance sends infinite extended variance to zero, so justify moment finiteness for the ordinary statistical interpretation. This marginal variance is not the directional long-run variance of epsilon_t times v_k^T X_t and does not prove that long-run variance is positive.

rows.query: Search Probability for sub-Weibull declarations; inspect the real exponential and real-power definitions against the scalar strict-tail inequality
rows.result: The exponential-power expression can be represented, but the inspected declarations do not supply a general sub-Weibull scalar tail class or the paper's inequality.
rows.gap: Define and establish the scalar noise tail inequality with its own positive scale and the stated shape range.

comparisons.D18: For every positive tau require P(abs epsilon_0 > tau) <= 2 exp(-(tau/C_epsilon)^gamma_2), with gamma_2 in (0,2] and absolute C_epsilon > 0. The base of the real power is positive, and the event is strict. This scale is not C_X; shared shape notation does not equate the two distributions. No independence from X_t or sub-Gaussian specialization for gamma_2 < 2 is introduced.

rows.query: Search Probability and Dynamics for functional dependence; inspect the real exponential-power and supremum-bound declarations for the directional cumulative L4 condition
rows.result: Checked real analysis primitives encode the all-lag bound; the direction-uniform cumulative functional-dependence coefficient itself has no verified packaged match.
rows.gap: Construct the direction-uniform cumulative L4 covariate dependence coefficients and prove their stated weighted all-lag bound.

comparisons.D13: Retain Delta^X_{m,4} as defined by the source's projection supremum and subsequent lag sum in (6)-(7). Multiply by exp(c m^gamma_1) and bound the supremum for all nonnegative integer m by the absolute positive D_X. This is not coordinatewise control, an L2 bound, or merely eventual decay. A real supremum formulation needs the boundedness and nonemptiness hypotheses of csSup_le_iff; pointwise all-lag bounds can instead be the predicate from which boundedness is proved.

rows.no_related_reason: The source introduces a particular scalar bookkeeping formula for combined dependence and tail exponents; searches found no declaration identifying that formula with this statistical role, and generic field arithmetic would not be a substantive library match.
rows.query: rg -i 'functional dependence|sub.?weibull|stationar.*causal|bernoulli shift' Mathlib/Probability Mathlib/Dynamics; compare the exact inverse-sum coefficient with the frozen source boundary
rows.result: No verified API was found for the combined product-process exponent; the formula can be defined directly using real inverses with positive parameters.
rows.gap: Define gamma as the inverse of gamma_1 inverse plus twice gamma_2 inverse and connect that specific exponent to the product-process bounds.

comparisons.D19: Preserve gamma = (gamma_1^(-1) + 2 gamma_2^(-1))^(-1), with the positive parameters furnished by the preceding assumptions. The factor two is essential and differs from the scalar gamma(Z) convention in Theorem 4. Shared gamma_1 and gamma_2 are chosen to cover covariate and error assumptions together; this does not identify their innovation processes or tail scales. Positivity of denominators is part of the intended real arithmetic interpretation.

rows.query: Inspect Real.log, Real.rpow and Filter.Tendsto; compare all factors and quantifiers in the source signal-spacing inequality (24)
rows.result: The logarithm, real exponent and divergence of a positive sequence can be encoded; no verified declaration gives the change-point signal-to-noise condition or a sufficient absolute constant.
rows.gap: Define the baseline signal-spacing assumption with the exact real exponent, minimum jump and spacing, and positive diverging sequence.

comparisons.D20: Require Delta times kappa squared >= C_snr times (s log(p n))^(2/gamma - 1) times alpha_n, with a sufficiently large absolute positive C_snr and alpha_n > 0 tending to positive infinity. Kappa and Delta are the two minima defined earlier. Coerce the positive sample size and dimension before taking log(p n), retaining the real-power convention at any zero base rather than assuming log(p n) is always strictly positive. Alpha_n is a growth sequence, not a significance level, and the stronger rate in part b is a separate addition.

rows.query: Inspect Analysis/Asymptotics/Defs IsLittleO and the real logarithm/power definitions; compare the faster-than condition with the retained baseline inequality
rows.result: The additional rate is expressible as a little-o relation at infinity; the checked declaration supplies the asymptotic predicate, not the paper's signal condition or its statistical consequence.
rows.gap: Combine the baseline inequality (24) with the little-o growth condition on the same alpha sequence.

comparisons.D21: Encode s(n) times (log(p(n) n))^(2/gamma) = o(alpha_n) atTop, with the positive alpha_n and baseline signal-spacing inequality from part a retained. Under the appropriate eventual positivity this corresponds to the displayed faster-than ratio. The exponent applies to log(p n), while s is outside that power; do not replace it by (s log(p n))^(2/gamma). This strengthens the same sequence used in (24) and is not merely divergence or an alternative that removes part a.

rows.query: Search Probability and Dynamics for causal functional-dependence constructions; inspect iid-family and measurable-map declarations with the source's time-dependent generator
rows.result: The iid innovations and measurable scalar maps have checked representations, but the lag-history causal process is not packaged by these declarations and a time-dependent generator does not yield stationarity.
rows.gap: Construct the generic scalar causal process from time-dependent measurable maps of its iid innovation histories while allowing nonstationarity.

comparisons.D10: Use integer-indexed iid zeta innovations and a measurable map g_t for each t to define Z_t from the history through t. Unlike G in (4) and g in (8), g_t may vary with time, so common innovation laws do not imply that Z_t has stationary finite-dimensional laws. The process is scalar and generic: do not import the regression model, sparsity, change points or a marginal zero mean that belongs to a later theorem's assumptions.
